newsitem.title: UK: Dollar steadies after surge to new peaks vs mark. [CORRECTED 08:39 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Dollar steadies after surge to new peaks vs mark. [CORRECTED 08:39 GMT]

text.p: The dollar paused for breath below the seven-and-a-half year high it set against the mark overnight, but was seen rallying further amid expectations the Bundesbank will not act anytime soon to curb mark weakness.
Mounting speculation that Europe's planned economic and monetary union will be launched by a broad group of countries has bolstered the dollar against the mark in recent weeks.

Signs that U.S. economic growth is continuing apace without stoking inflation has, however, generated demand for U.S. stocks and bonds and helped the dollar gain against other major currencies like the Swiss franc and the yen.

"There has been a shift from the mark weakness story to an independent dollar strength story, and people are going to stick to this trend," said Mark Geddes, treasury economist at ABN Amro. "We will doubtless get the threat of intervention and rhetoric out of Germany but the Bundesbank is unlikely to hike the repo rate unless the dollar is travelling at speed above 1.90 (marks)."

The dollar hit 1.8470 marks overnight, the strongest it has been since November 1989 when it reached 1.8690. It also leapt to 1.5250 Swiss francs, its best showing since August 1993. Dollar/yen climbed to a two-month high of 117.42.
Dollar/mark was at 1.8426/36 at 0755 GMT from 1.8354/64 late Friday in Europe. The U.S. currency was at 117.27/37 yen and at 1.5180/90 Swiss francs from 116.70/80 and 1.5128/38 on Friday.
Bundesbank officials have already launched the war of words with currency traders.

Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, vice president of the German central bank, said in an interview last week that the dollar was slightly overvalued. Also, his fellow council member Reimut Jochimsen said the Bundesbank, which did not normally allow exchange rates to dictate its policy, was following exchange more closely than usual.

"The market does not believe the Bundesbank for a second in terms of its willingness or its ability to support the mark," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

The mark was offered temporary support last week amid talk the Bundesbank could switch to using variable-rate tenders to set the securities repurchase rate from the fixed-rate tenders it has been using to keep the repo rate frozen at 3.0 percent (corrects from 3.30 percent) since August 1996.
Such talk proved to be unfounded and emboldened traders to drive the dollar to new heights against the mark.
